title: Data-response questions
examples: When I look at this graph, what should I say first?
How do I move from just describing numbers to explaining them?
Is it always okay to just point at the graph and say what you see?

explain.say: Today we will learn to answer questions about data very well. We will learn to describe, explain, and use figures.

items: Explain: Why the data might be changing (why)
Use Figures: Pointing to specific numbers (where)

explain.say: First we must describe what the data is doing. This means stating the key features you see. For example, the temperature rose from ten degrees to twenty degrees.

draw.text: Describe: State what the data shows.

explain.say: Next we must explain the data. This means suggesting a reason for the pattern. For example, the rise might be due to global warming.
Finally we must use figures to support our points. This means quoting exact numbers from the graph. For example, the increase was about ten degrees over three years.
In everyday life we see this when looking at news reports. If the report shows falling sales, you should describe the drop, explain why it might happen, and use the exact percentage figures.
A common mistake is only describing the data without explaining it. You just say what you see, but you do not say why it is happening.

items: Always link your description to a reason.

faq.q: Do I have to say everything I see on the graph?
faq.a: No, you only need to mention the most important trends. Look for the biggest changes or the clearest patterns.
asks: Should I mention every single point?
What is the most important thing to focus on?

faq.q: When should I explain the data versus just describing it?
faq.a: You describe the facts first, stating what the numbers are doing. Then, you explain by suggesting a possible cause for that trend.
asks: Is there a specific order I must follow?
What is the difference between describing and explaining?

faq.q: How do I know which figures to use?
faq.a: Use figures when you need to make your point stronger. Pick numbers that show the biggest difference or the clearest change.
asks: Should I use averages or specific points?
Can I use more than two numbers?

faq.q: Can I use my own knowledge when I explain the data?
faq.a: Yes, you can suggest reasons based on what you know. Remember to use words like 'suggests' so it sounds like an educated guess.
asks: Is it okay to guess the reason?
How do I phrase a guess correctly?

faq.q: If the data is messy, what should I do?
faq.a: If the data is messy, describe the general pattern, like 'fluctuating' or 'erratic'. Then, explain that the data might be unpredictable.
asks: What if there is no clear pattern?
How do I talk about random numbers?

facts: Description involves stating what the data shows, such as an increase or decrease.
Explanation involves suggesting a possible cause or reason for the observed pattern.
Using figures means quoting specific numbers or percentages from the source.
A good response moves logically from what is seen to why it might be happening.

quiz.say: A graph shows sales rising from 100 units to 500 units over five years. What is the best initial step?

options.show: Explain: This must be because of a new marketing campaign.
options.say: Explain: This must be because of a new marketing campaign.

options.show: Use Figures: The increase was 400 units over five years.
options.say: Use Figures: The increase was 400 units over five years.

options.show: Compare: Sales were low in year one and high in year five.
options.say: Compare: Sales were low in year one and high in year five.

quiz.why: This correctly states the factual change seen in the data.

wrong.0: This jumps straight to an explanation without first stating the visible data trend.
wrong.1: This only uses figures and misses the initial description of the trend.
wrong.2: This is a comparison, but the first step must be a simple, direct description of the overall trend.

quiz.say: If data shows a pattern that slows down over time, what should your explanation suggest?
quiz.show: Explain: The rate of change is decreasing.

options.show: It must be due to external factors.
options.say: It must be due to external factors.

options.show: The rate of change is decreasing.
options.say: The rate of change is decreasing.

options.show: The total amount is lower than expected.
options.say: The total amount is lower than expected.

options.show: It was low in the beginning and high at the end.
options.say: It was low in the beginning and high at the end.

quiz.why: This correctly explains the pattern of change, not just the final numbers.

wrong.0: This is too vague; a good explanation suggests a specific type of factor.
wrong.2: This is a judgment, not an explanation of the rate of change itself.
wrong.3: This is a simple description, not an explanation of the slowing trend.
